question: Systematic evasion of sanctions against Russia and use of the EU anticircumvention mechanism

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU has adopted successive sanctions packages designed to limit Russian access to dual-use goods with military applications. However, analyses based on trade statistics show that, while direct exports from the EU to Russia have fallen, exports of those goods to certain third countries have risen exponentially, pointing to systematic sanctions evasion through re-exports.

Article 12f of the 11th package of sanctions, adopted in June 2023, introduced an anticircumventing instrument that enables the EU to ban exports to third countries that fail to actively prevent the re-export of sanctioned goods to Russia, but to date, the mechanism remains unused. 1.
In the light of the documented increase in re-exports to Russia, does the Commission consider the current approach to combating sanctions evasion to be effective?
Will the Commission apply Article 12f to third countries that have systematically and persistently failed to prevent re-exports of that kind?
What will the Commission do to ensure that the enforcement of sanctions is not undermined by a lack of political will or insufficient checks within the EU itself?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2026) Addressing circumvention of sanctions, which is now a crime under EU law, is a key priority for the EU.

The Commission monitors trade flows, especially goods on the Common High Priority1 and Economically Critical Goods2 lists, from the EU to third countries considered to be at high risk of being used as a platform for circumvention, and from these countries to Russia. The EU has several anti-circumvention tools at its disposal.

These include imposing sanctions on individuals and entities facilitating circumvention of EU sanctions as per Council Decision 2014/145/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 269/20143, strengthening export controls towards entities involved in the circumvention of sensitive items to Russia4, or the prohibition on export of sensitive goods to a country whose jurisdiction is used to circumvent EU sanctions5.

The Commission remains determined to fight sanctions evasion and will continue its rigorous monitoring of trade flows and targeted outreach on the issue of sanctions circumvention and will not hesitate to propose any measures considered necessary.

Particular importance is placed on monitoring trade flows which show that EU exports of sensitive goods to third countries are at high risk of re-export to Russia, thus circumventing existing export restrictions. In this context, the Commission can propose to activate the Anti-Circumvention Tool (Article 12(f) of the Council Regulation (EU) 833/2014).
The Council decides unanimously on the amendment or adoption of new sanctions.

1 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/list-common-high-priority-items_en. 2 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/list-economically-critical-goods_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2014/145(1)/2025-12-15 and https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/269/oj/eng. 4 Annex IV of Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/833/oj/eng. 5 Article 12f of Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014.
